summary: This unit teaches you to organise the finances of a small business so that you always know where the money is and what is owed. You will learn to keep business and personal money apart, keep records and source documents, run petty cash and bank reconciliations, forecast cash flow, control debtors and creditors, meet tax and payroll obligations, read basic financial statements and choose sensible sources of finance.

blocks.p: A small business can be profitable and still fail because its owner does not know how much cash is coming in and going out, who owes money and when bills are due. Organising business finances means building simple, regular habits and systems so that the owner can make decisions with correct figures. The unit is for owners and managers of small businesses and for staff who keep their records.

A **written paper**: short answers (terms like imprest, TRN, drawings, unpresented cheque, cash book) and longer answers.
**Group practical tasks**: organising one month of a small business's records, and preparing a six-month cash flow forecast with a finance plan.

blocks.note: This unit uses **J$**, and GCT and statutory deductions **at the current rate**. Never invent a rate in an answer: use the figures you are given, or write 'at the current rate'.

sections.title: Records, source documents and the bookkeeping system

blocks.h: Keep business and personal money apart

blocks.p: A small business owner who pays business bills from her personal account, or puts takings into it, **mixes the records and hides the true business position**. She cannot tell the profit, cannot prove expenses and makes it hard for the bank and tax authority to trust the figures. The fix is simple:

ul: Open a **separate business bank account**. Pay all takings into it and all business bills from it.
Pay the owner by recorded **drawings** (a sole trader takes money out of the business for personal use) or a salary, not by dipping into the till.
Keep a receipt for every expense. A business that pays personal items from business funds must record them as drawings, not expenses.

blocks.p: Every entry in the books must be backed by a **source document**: the paper or file that proves a transaction took place.

head: Transaction
Source document
rows: Sales invoice (a copy of the one sent to the customer)
Till roll, cash receipt or receipt book copy
Receipt, cheque stub or bank transfer record
Receipt issued and bank deposit slip
Signed petty cash voucher with receipt

blocks.p: Receipts prove expenses for **tax and checks**. Without them, an expense may be refused, and errors cannot be traced.

blocks.h: Double-entry bookkeeping and the chart of accounts

blocks.p: In **double-entry bookkeeping**, each transaction is recorded twice: as a **debit** in one account and a **credit** in another, so the books always balance. A **chart of accounts** is a list of account names and codes used for recording: for example sales, purchases, wages, rent, utilities, transport, equipment, bank, debtors and creditors. Choose names that fit your business so that reports are meaningful.
The **cash book** is the record of all cash and bank receipts and payments. Many small businesses use accounting software or a spreadsheet to keep it.

head: Event
How it is recorded
rows: Owner takes J$50,000 for personal use
Drawings (reduces the owner's equity); not an expense, not sales
Capital expenditure: an asset, depreciated over its life
Revenue expenditure: an expense of the month
Money in; the customer's debt falls

ul: Software speeds up recording, reduces arithmetic errors and gives **current reports**, such as profit and aged debtors. It does not remove the need to keep receipts, pay tax or check the figures.
A business that keeps all its accounts on one computer must **back up regularly to a second secure place**, and protect the data with passwords. Never leave the device in a car overnight.
Keep records for the **period that tax and company law require**, which is longer than a month or a year. Ask your accountant for the current period.

sections.title: Cash handling, petty cash and internal controls

blocks.p: **Petty cash** pays small, everyday costs: postage, tea, a taxi fare. The usual system is the **imprest system**: a fixed float is set, for example J$15,000. Each payment is supported by a **signed voucher with a receipt**. At the end of the period the cash left plus the vouchers must equal the float, and the cashier draws from the bank **only the amount spent** to restore the float.

head: Step
Example
rows: Cash that should be in the box
Cash to add to restore the float

blocks.p: If the box holds J$3,520 instead of J$3,720, there is an unexplained shortage of J$200, which must be recorded and investigated.

blocks.note: Good petty cash controls: one named custodian, the box kept locked, a signed voucher and receipt for every payment, a limit on single payments, surprise checks by someone else, and the float restored regularly. An open drawer, a note-it-later system or counting once a year are all poor controls.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Count cash takings with two people, record them and bank them daily. Cash kept on the premises can be stolen, lost or borrowed. Keep banking slips and match them to the sales records.

**Internal controls** are the checks that protect money and records from error and fraud. The most important is **separation of duties**: no one person should handle a transaction from start to finish. For example, the person who writes cheques should not also record them and reconcile the bank.

head: Control
Example in a small office
rows: One person receives and records sales; another (or the owner) prepares the bank reconciliation
The owner approves every payment, with the invoice checked first
Cash takings counted by two people
Passwords on accounting software; only some staff can change entries
Surprise petty cash counts; owner reviews the bank statement
Cover for fire, theft and other losses

blocks.p: **Warning signs of possible fraud:** missing receipts, unexplained cash shortages, a person who never takes leave, a reluctance to let others see the books, and reconciliations that are always late. Taking a full block of annual leave is **not** a warning sign: a long absence is a good test of a system.
With only two or three staff, full separation is hard. Use the owner's review as the extra control: she looks at the bank statement and approves payments.

A **bank reconciliation** matches the **cash book** to the **bank statement** at the end of each month. The two rarely agree for ordinary reasons, and any difference that you cannot explain may be an error or fraud. Doing it monthly means that errors are found while they are small.

head: Item
In cash book?
On bank statement?
Action
rows: Direct debit, standing order or customer transfer
Unpresented cheque (written and recorded but not yet paid by the bank)
List; deduct from the bank balance
Deposit not yet credited (banked at month end but not yet shown)
List; add to the bank balance
Error by the bank or by the firm
Correct it, and tell the bank if theirs

flow: Get the bank statement and cash book for the same period
Tick off items that appear in both
Items on the statement but not in the cash book: check, then enter them in the cash book
Work out the corrected cash book balance
List items in the cash book but not on the statement: unpresented cheques and deposits not yet credited
Adjust the bank statement balance for those items
The two adjusted balances must agree; if not, look for errors

blocks.p: A Black River boat-tour company has a cash book balance of **J$186,400** and a bank statement balance of **J$214,900**. Differences found: bank charges of J$2,100 and a customer transfer of J$6,000 on the statement but not in the cash book; two cheques (J$21,000 and J$15,500) not yet presented; a deposit of J$11,900 banked on the last day and not yet credited.
The two sides agree at J$190,300. The reconciliation is complete. Always check the sum twice: 186,400 − 2,100 + 6,000 = 190,300; 214,900 − 36,500 + 11,900 = 190,300.

blocks.note: A cheque written on 30 June that reaches the bank in July is an **unpresented cheque** in the June reconciliation. It is not a bank error, a bank charge or a deposit.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Profit** is counted when a sale is made. **Cash** moves when money arrives or leaves. A business can make a profit and still run out of cash because:

ul: Customers have 30 or 60 days to pay, but wages, rent and suppliers must be paid now.
Cash is tied up in **stock** that has not sold.
Cash goes into loan repayments, new equipment and the owner's drawings, which do not reduce profit in the same way.
A fast-growing business buys stock and hires staff before customers pay.

blocks.p: A furniture maker who made a profit last quarter but cannot pay this month's wages usually has cash tied up in unpaid invoices and stock.

A **cash flow forecast** shows the money expected to come in and go out, month by month, so the owner can see problems before they happen. It is a tool for the future; the income statement is a look back at profit; the balance sheet shows the position on one date.

head: Line
Month 1 (J$)
Month 2 (J$)
rows: Net cash for the month (receipts − payments)

blocks.p: Closing cash = opening cash + receipts − payments. Month 1: 90,000 + 380,000 − 455,000 = **15,000**. Month 2 opens with that 15,000: 15,000 + 410,000 − 400,000 = **25,000**. Month 1 is dangerously low, so the owner must act: collect debts sooner, delay a non-urgent purchase, ask for supplier terms or arrange a short-term overdraft before the problem arrives.
Build a forecast by estimating **when cash actually moves**, not when sales are made. If a customer pays 30 days after the invoice, a March sale appears as cash in April.

**Working capital** = current assets − current liabilities. It is the money available to run the business day to day. A boutique with J$2,000,000 of slow-selling stock has cash **tied up** that could pay bills. Money locked in unsold stock does not pay wages.
Example: current assets J$1,260,000 and current liabilities J$840,000. Working capital = 1,260,000 − 840,000 = **J$420,000**. Current ratio = 1,260,000 ÷ 840,000 = **1.5 : 1**.

blocks.note: Ways to protect cash: invoice promptly, chase debts early, keep stock lean, negotiate supplier terms, forecast regularly, and keep a safe minimum cash level.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Credit control** is managing the money customers owe so that it is collected on time. Customers who owe the business money are **debtors** (receivables). Suppliers to whom the business owes money are **creditors** (payables).

flow: Before the sale: check the customer, take references, set a credit limit and agree terms in writing
Send accurate invoices promptly, showing the due date and payment details
Each week, review an aged debtors report
A few days before the due date, send a polite reminder to large accounts
When late: a polite reminder, then a phone call, then a firm letter
Persistent non-payment: stop further credit, agree a payment plan or take legal advice
Write off a debt only as the last step and with the owner's approval

blocks.p: An **aged debtors report** shows how long each customer's invoice has been unpaid, usually in bands: current, 1 to 30 days late, 31 to 60, over 60. It lets you chase the oldest and biggest debts first.

Customer C is the priority: all of its debt is more than a month late. A customer 45 days late on a 30-day invoice should first receive a **polite reminder and a phone call**, not an immediate write-off, a penalty added without notice or a stop on all supply to everyone.

A useful measure of credit control is overdue debts as a percentage of sales. If overdue debts are J$360,000 on sales of J$4,800,000, they are 360,000 ÷ 4,800,000 × 100 = **7.5%**. A good goal is specific and measurable, such as 'reduce overdue debts to below 5% of sales in six months'.

Pay on the **due date**, not early and not late, unless a discount makes early payment worth it. A supplier who offers 2% off for payment within 10 days is giving a very high return: on an invoice of J$250,000, the discount is 250,000 × 2 ÷ 100 = J$5,000, so you pay J$245,000. If the business has spare cash, take the discount. Keep a calendar of bills due so that nothing is paid late by accident. Paying late risks supplier trust and loss of credit terms.

blocks.note: Never fund your own late payments with money withheld for tax, payroll deductions or staff pay. These are legal obligations and have penalties.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Jamaican businesses must keep proper records and meet several tax and statutory duties. The rates and thresholds change, so use the **current** figures from Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ) or your accountant. This kit never gives a rate: use 'at the current rate'.

head: Obligation
What it means
rows: The number a business and its employees quote in all dealings with TAJ and in many bank and statutory matters.
The business (or owner) files returns on its profits each year and pays tax by the due dates.

A tax on most goods and services. A GCT-registered business charges it to customers at the current rate, keeps its sales and purchase invoices, files returns and pays the tax over on time. It may claim back **input tax** on its purchases, but only with valid purchase invoices to support the claim.
Employers deduct income tax from wages and pay it over.
Contributions by employer and employee that fund pensions and other benefits.
Deducted from pay and paid over, with an employer share.

blocks.h: What an employer must do with deductions

blocks.p: PAYE, NIS, NHT and Education Tax are called **statutory deductions**. The employer takes them from employees' pay and also pays its own share where the law requires. It must **pay them over, with returns, by the due dates**. It must not keep them as working capital or use them to pay suppliers when cash is short. The money belongs to the state.

For each employee, record every pay period: **gross pay**, each deduction, and **net pay**. Net pay = gross pay − deductions. Example: gross J$80,000, total statutory deductions J$17,500 (shown on the payslip) gives net **J$62,500**. Keep the payroll summary as the source document for wages.
A calendar of statutory dates, kept by one person with a back-up, avoids missing a deadline. Paying late brings penalties and interest, and can lead to action.

blocks.note: GCT collected from customers is **not** the business's income. It is money owed to the state, less valid input tax. Keep it in view in the cash flow forecast.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Statement
Shows
When
rows: Over a period, such as a month or a year
Cash coming in and going out
The record of cash and bank receipts and payments

blocks.p: **Gross profit** = sales − cost of goods sold. **Net profit** = gross profit − expenses. **Gross profit margin** = gross profit ÷ sales × 100.

The **current ratio** = current assets ÷ current liabilities. A ratio of 1.5 : 1 means J$1.50 of current assets for every J$1 owed in the short term. A fall from 1.8 : 1 to 0.9 : 1 in a year suggests the firm **may struggle to pay its short-term debts**. A ratio below 1 : 1 is a warning.

**Capital expenditure** buys assets that last more than a year: a van, an oven, equipment. **Revenue expenditure** pays the running costs of the period: electricity, wages, flour. **Depreciation** spreads the cost of a physical asset over its life. Straight-line: (cost − expected resale value) ÷ number of years.

Worked example: a van costs J$3,500,000, will be used for 6 years and then sold for about J$500,000. Yearly depreciation = (3,500,000 − 500,000) ÷ 6 = 3,000,000 ÷ 6 = **J$500,000**. Check: 500,000 × 6 = 3,000,000, and 3,500,000 − 3,000,000 = 500,000.

blocks.note: Depreciation is a non-cash expense: it reduces profit but does not take cash out of the bank. This is one reason profit and cash differ.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Finance, advice, insurance and the monthly routine

head: Source
Best for
Points to watch
rows: A temporary gap, such as buying Christmas stock that sells within weeks
Often costly; the bank can reduce or withdraw it quickly
Late payment harms trust; discounts may be lost
Repayments are fixed; interest costs; security may be needed
Long term, secured on the property
Growth, when borrowing is too risky
The investor shares ownership and profit; the owner gives up some control

blocks.p: The golden rule is to **match the term of the finance to the life of the need**: short-term needs with short-term finance, long-term assets with long-term finance. A key difference: **a loan is repaid, with interest; equity gives a share of ownership.**

ul: **Insurance** protects against loss from fire, theft, flood and liability. Keep cover suitable and up to date.

An **accountant** helps set up the systems, advises on tax and prepares year-end accounts. Seek advice when setting up, when tax is unclear, before major finance decisions and for year-end accounts: not only when the business is in trouble or after a letter from the tax authority.

flow: Record all invoices, receipts, bank items and payroll for last month
Reconcile the bank and petty cash
Review the aged debtors report and chase overdue accounts
List bills and statutory payments due next month
Update the cash flow forecast
Review key figures against targets and note actions

blocks.p: **Set financial goals** that are specific, measurable and time-bound: 'Cut overdue debts to under 10% of sales in 6 months' is a good goal; 'do better with the bank' is not. A fixed monthly routine turns finance from a crisis into a habit.

c1.title: A Savanna-la-Mar bakery's petty cash
c1.text: Joy Reid owns a bakery in Savanna-la-Mar. She pays supplier bills from her personal account and puts the weekly takings in the same account. Her shop assistant looks after a petty cash float of J$15,000. This week's signed vouchers total J$11,280. Joy has noticed that J$200 is missing from the box and that no one else ever checks it.

c2.title: A Black River boat-tour company
c2.text: A Black River boat-tour company has a cash book balance of J$186,400 at the end of the month. The bank statement shows J$214,900. The statement includes bank charges of J$2,100 and a customer transfer of J$6,000 not yet in the cash book. Two cheques for J$21,000 and J$15,500 have not been presented, and a deposit of J$11,900 made on the last day is not yet credited.

c3.title: A Christiana farm-produce supplier
c3.text: A farm-produce supplier in Christiana, Manchester, started the month with J$90,000 in the bank. It expects to collect J$380,000 and to pay out J$455,000. It sells to hotels on 30-day terms and its biggest customer is 45 days late. The owner, Mr Delroy Bailey, is offered a discount of 2% by a packaging supplier for payment within 10 days on a J$250,000 invoice, and has spare cash from a good previous month.

c4.title: A Kingston courier firm
c4.text: A Kingston courier company had sales of J$2,400,000 last quarter and cost of goods sold of J$1,560,000. Its expenses were J$600,000. Current assets are J$1,260,000 and current liabilities are J$840,000. It has just bought a delivery van for J$3,500,000, expected to be used for 6 years and then sold for about J$500,000.

c5.title: A Portmore garment workshop
c5.text: A Portmore garment workshop has four office and sewing staff. The owner, Ms Tanya Brown, wants to buy new sewing machines costing J$1,800,000. One employee, Carlton, receives the cash takings, writes the receipts, records them in the books and does the bank reconciliation. He has not taken leave in three years. The workshop has no insurance, and the cash book is kept only on one laptop.

questions.q: What is the main problem with Joy paying business bills from her personal account?
o: It is against the law and she must stop doing it at once
It mixes the records and hides the real business position
It means the bank will charge her higher fees every month
It will make her customers pay their bills later than due
questions.why: Mixing records means Joy cannot tell the business profit, cannot prove expenses and cannot control cash. The fix is a separate business account, with the owner paid by recorded drawings.

questions.q: How much cash must be drawn from the bank to restore the J$15,000 petty cash float?
questions.why: Under the imprest system only the amount spent is restored: 11,280. The box should hold 15,000 − 11,280 = J$3,720 before the top-up.

questions.q: The box holds J$3,520 when it should hold J$3,720. What should happen?
o: Record the shortage, investigate and add outside checks
Add J$200 from the till so that the box balances again
Ignore the amount because it is so small to matter
Dismiss the assistant at once because she keeps the box
questions.why: An unexplained shortage should never be hidden by topping it up from elsewhere. Record it, investigate and strengthen controls, such as surprise counts by someone else, signed vouchers and a limit per payment.

questions.q: Why does the bakery restore its petty cash on the imprest system rather than topping up from the till when needed?
o: It avoids the need for vouchers on small payments
It allows bills to be paid from the box when cash is short
A fixed float shows any shortage when it is restored
It removes the need for anyone to check the cash
questions.why: Under the imprest system the cash left plus vouchers must always equal the float, so a shortage or missing voucher is revealed at each restoration. Vouchers are still required, and the box is not for paying bills.

questions.q: How should the customer transfer of J$6,000 on the bank statement be treated in the reconciliation?
o: Deduct it from the balance on the bank statement
Ignore it, since the bank already has the money
Enter it in the cash book as a receipt
Report it to the bank as an error it has made
questions.why: A receipt shown on the statement but missing from the cash book must be entered in the cash book. After that, the corrected cash book balance is 186,400 − 2,100 + 6,000 = J$190,300.

questions.q: What is the adjusted bank balance after taking account of the unpresented cheques and the deposit not yet credited?
questions.why: 214,900 − 36,500 + 11,900 = 190,300. Unpresented cheques are deducted and deposits not yet credited are added to the bank balance. The two sides now agree.

questions.q: How should the two unpresented cheques be treated in the reconciliation?
o: They are entered a second time as new payments
They are reported to the bank as its own errors
They are added to the balance on the bank statement
They are listed and deducted from the bank balance
questions.why: They are already in the cash book but have not reached the bank, so they are timing differences that reduce the bank balance. They are neither a bank error nor a new payment.

questions.q: Why should the company reconcile the bank every month?
o: To ask the bank to approve a higher overdraft limit
To find errors and fraud while they are small
To work out the profit made for the whole year
To pay all of its suppliers at one and the same time
questions.why: A monthly reconciliation proves that the cash book is accurate and exposes unexplained items early. It is not a profit calculation or a request to the bank.

questions.q: What is the expected closing cash for the month?
questions.why: 90,000 + 380,000 − 455,000 = J$15,000. Closing cash = opening cash + receipts − payments.

questions.q: The closing cash is very low. Which action is most sensible?
o: Pay the suppliers late without telling any of them
Chase late debts and delay purchases that are not urgent
Take the owner's drawings from the business as usual this month
Stop recording the cash flow forecast until things improve
questions.why: Speeding up collection and delaying non-urgent spending protects cash. Paying late harms trust, drawings drain cash and stopping the forecast removes the early warning.

questions.q: What is the best first step with the biggest customer, which is 45 days late on a 30-day invoice?
o: Send a polite reminder and phone the customer
Write the debt off as a loss at once
Stop supplying every customer until it pays
Add a large penalty to the bill without notice
questions.why: The first step with a late payer is a polite reminder and a call, followed by firmer steps if needed. Write-offs, blanket stops and unannounced penalties are premature and damage relationships.

questions.q: Should Mr Bailey take the 2% discount for payment within 10 days, and how much would he pay?
o: No, because discounts are too small to matter; he would pay J$250,000
Yes, but he would pay J$247,500
Yes, because he has spare cash; he would pay J$245,000
No, because paying late is always better; he would pay J$250,000
questions.why: 2% of 250,000 = 5,000, so he pays 245,000. A discount for paying about 20 days early is a very high return, so with spare cash it is wise to take it.

questions.q: What is the courier firm's gross profit margin?
What is the net profit?
questions.why: Net profit = gross profit − expenses = 840,000 − 600,000 = J$240,000.

questions.q: What is the yearly straight-line depreciation on the van?
questions.why: (3,500,000 − 500,000) ÷ 6 = J$500,000. The expected resale value is deducted before dividing by the years of use.

questions.q: What is the current ratio, and what does it suggest?
o: 0.67 : 1, so it may struggle to pay its debts
1.5 : 1, so it is making a net loss
0.67 : 1, so it has plenty of spare cash
1.5 : 1, so it can meet its short-term debts
questions.why: 1,260,000 ÷ 840,000 = 1.5 : 1. The firm has J$1.50 of current assets for each J$1 of short-term debt, so it is likely to be able to pay.

questions.q: Carlton receives cash, writes receipts, records them and does the bank reconciliation. Which control is missing?
o: Depreciation of the equipment
Separation of duties
Credit control for customers
Budgeting for next year
questions.why: One person handles the transaction from start to finish, so errors or theft could go unnoticed. The owner or another person should do the reconciliation, and cash should be counted by two people.

questions.q: Which fact about Carlton is the strongest warning sign of possible fraud, together with the lack of controls?
o: He has taken no leave for three years
He works in the office all day long
He is the one who receives the takings
He knows the customers very well indeed
questions.why: A person who never takes leave may be preventing others from seeing his work. Combined with no separation of duties, this is a classic warning sign.

questions.q: Ms Brown wants to buy sewing machines costing J$1,800,000. Which source of finance fits best?
o: A bank overdraft that is repaid within a few weeks
Supplier credit on terms of a few weeks only
A petty cash float that is topped up each week
A term loan matched to the machines' life
questions.why: Equipment lasts for years, so medium-term finance such as a term loan is the best fit. Overdrafts and short credit are for temporary gaps.

questions.q: What should the workshop do about its single laptop and lack of insurance?
o: Print everything and then delete the files from the laptop
Share the laptop password with all staff in case of need, for safety
Back up the accounts to a second place and take out insurance
Rely on the accountant to rebuild the records after any loss
questions.why: Regular backups to a second secure location protect the records, and insurance protects the business against loss from fire or theft. Sharing passwords or relying on rebuilding records leaves the firm exposed.
